Challah is a special type of bread deeply rooted in Jewish tradition. It is made from a soft, slightly sweet, egg-enriched dough — meaning eggs are mixed directly into the dough, which gives the bread a rich, tender texture and a mild golden-yellow color on the inside. The outside crust is shiny and golden-brown, achieved by brushing the dough with egg before baking.

The most recognizable form of challah is a braided loaf — strands of dough are twisted and woven together (like braiding hair) before baking, creating a beautiful, patterned shape. Three strands braided together is the most common style, though loaves with four, six, or even more strands exist, each producing a different visual pattern. The end result looks elegant, almost like a decorative centerpiece.

For Rosh Hashanah (the Jewish New Year), challah is shaped differently — instead of a long braid, the dough is coiled into a round spiral. This circular shape carries meaning: it represents the cycle of the year and the hope for a sweet, full year ahead.

Challah is soft, pillowy, and slightly sweet — richer and more flavourful than plain white bread, but lighter than a heavily buttery bread like brioche. It has a gentle pull when you tear it apart, and the inside is fluffy. Some versions include raisins mixed into the dough, especially the round Rosh Hashanah variety.

Challah is most closely associated with Shabbat, the Jewish day of rest that begins at sundown on Friday and ends on Saturday night. Every Friday evening, it is traditional to place two whole loaves of challah on the dinner table. These two loaves are not arbitrary — they represent a story from Jewish scripture: when the Israelites wandered the desert, God sent "manna" (heavenly food) from the sky for them to collect each day. On Fridays, He sent a double portion so they wouldn't need to collect any on the Sabbath. The two loaves of challah are a weekly re-enactment of this miracle.

Before eating, the loaves are typically covered with a special cloth and then uncovered at the right moment during the Friday night ritual. A blessing over bread (known as HaMotzi) is recited, and then the bread is torn or sliced and shared among everyone at the table. This ritual transforms an ordinary meal into something ceremonial and meaningful.

Challah also appears at other Jewish holidays — on Purim, Sukkot, and other festive occasions — and is essentially the bread of celebration in Jewish life.
A Jewish Law Connected to the Name

In Jewish law, whenever a significant amount of dough is prepared, the baker is required to set aside a small portion of that dough. This separated piece is also called challah in Hebrew. This ritual act — separating a piece of dough — is where the bread itself gets its name. The bread is named after this very practice of "taking challah" from the dough.

Because challah is so soft and slightly sweet, it has also become popular in everyday cooking far outside of strictly Jewish contexts. It is widely sold in bakeries worldwide. People use it to make exceptional French toast (its richness soaks up egg and milk beautifully), bread pudding, and sandwiches. Many people who have no connection to Jewish traditions simply enjoy it as a high-quality, delicious bread.

Challah is a braided, egg-enriched, slightly sweet bread that sits at the heart of Jewish religious and family life — present at the Shabbat table every week, reshaped into a circle on the New Year, and cherished both as a sacred ritual object and as a genuinely delicious food. It is soft and golden, beautiful to look at, and rich with centuries of meaning.
